slides.title: Process Creation
slides.notes: First of all we will start with the Process Creation

slides.title: Every Process Is Born From Another Process
slides.body:
The Parent–Child Idea
A running process (the parent) creates a new process (the child) using the fork() system call
In Linux/Unix, this is the primary way new processes are made
The child starts as an almost-exact copy of the parent, then the two run independently
slides.notes: let's understand how new processes are created. Every process is typically created by another process, known as its parent. In Linux and Unix systems, this happens using the fork() system call. The newly created child process initially receives a copy of the parent's state, but after creation, both parent and child execute independently and can perform different tasks.

slides.title: fork() - One Call, Two Processes
slides.notes: Now, let's see what makes fork() unique. Although it is called only once, it creates two running processes—the original parent and the new child. After the fork() call, both processes continue execution from the next line of code, allowing them to run independently while starting from the same point.

slides.title: fork() - One Call, Two Processes
slides.notes: Next, the return value of fork() helps each process identify its role. The child process receives 0, while the parent receives the Process ID, or PID, of the child, which is always a positive value. If the process creation fails, fork() returns -1, indicating that no child process was created.

slides.title: fork() - One Call, Two Processes
slides.body:
Called Once But Returns Twice
pid = fork();   if (pid == 0)

slides.notes: Moving on, this code shows the common way to use fork(). After calling fork(), we check its return value. If the value is 0, the code inside the child block executes. If it is greater than 0, the parent process executes its block. If the value is -1, it means an error occurred and the child process was not created.

slides.title: fork() - One Call, Two Processes
slides.body:
Example
Python
import os
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
   print("Hello from CHILD")
else:
   print("Hello from PARENT", pid)
Possible Output 1
Hello from PARENT 283
Hello from CHILD
Possible Output 2
Hello from CHILD
Hello from PARENT 283
Output
slides.notes: NOte : Pid ,  changes from run to run.The operating system assigns an available PID whenever it creates a new process. Since different processes are created and terminated over time, the next available PID is usually different.

slides.title: fork() - One Call, Two Processes
slides.notes: Now, after fork() executes, both the parent and child run independently, so both print their respective messages. Since they execute concurrently, the order of the output is not fixed. Sometimes the parent prints first, and other times the child does, depending on how the operating system schedules them.

slides.title: fork() - One Call, Two Processes
slides.notes: Like photocopying yourself — now there are two of you. A name tag tells you apart: the original reads 'parent,' the copy reads 'child.' That tag is the return value: the child sees 0, the parent sees the child's ID.

slides.title: What Does the Child Get From the Parent?
tables: Its own copy of the parent’s memory
Copied - so it resumes at the same point
New and unique - the child is its own process
Shared - both point to the same open file

slides.title: What Does the Child Get From the Parent?
slides.notes: Going forward, when a child process is created, it inherits most of the parent's resources, such as memory, files, and process information. However, modern operating systems use a technique called copy-on-write, where memory is not copied immediately. Instead, a copy is created only if either process modifies the data, making fork() much faster and more efficient.

slides.title: Parent and Child
slides.notes: Parent and child are like identical twins: same starting “DNA” (memory), but separate identities (PIDs) and separate lives from birth.

slides.title: Processes Form a Family Tree
slides.body:
Every process Has Exactly One Parent
Because processes are created by other processes, they form a tree (hierarchy)
Every process has one parent but can have many children
The first process is init / systemd (PID 1), started at the end of booting - the ancestor of every other process
Each process is identified by its PID and remembers its parent via its PPID
(init)
slides.notes: Next, processes in an operating system are organized like a family tree. Every process has one parent, but it can create multiple child processes. At the top of this hierarchy is the init or systemd process with PID 1, which is created during system startup and acts as the ancestor of all other processes. Each process is uniquely identified by its PID and also stores its Parent Process ID, or PPID.Analogy: A family tree: one common ancestor (init), everyone has exactly one parent but can have many children. Trace anyone’s parents upward and you reach init.

slides.title: Running a Program
slides.notes: Next we will learn about Running a Program

slides.title: exec() - Replace the Program, Keep the Process
slides.notes: Now, exec() works differently from fork(). It doesn’t create a new process; instead, it overwrites the current process with a new program. The process ID stays the same, but everything else—code, data, and memory—is replaced. Once exec() succeeds, the original program is gone, so it never returns back to the old code. Different variants like execl, execv, and others just change how arguments are passed and whether the system searches the PATH automatically.

slides.title: exec() - Replace the Program, Keep the Process
slides.notes: Like switching the app on your phone: same phone (same process), but tap a new app and the whole screen becomes something else (new program). The device doesn't change — what it's running does.

slides.title: fork() + exec() - Create, Then Run
slides.notes: Moving on, fork() and exec() are often used together in real systems. fork() creates a new child process, but at that point both parent and child are still running the same program. Usually, that’s not what we want. So the child process then calls exec() to replace itself with a completely different program. In simple terms, fork() is used to create a new process, and exec() is used to load and run a new program inside it.

slides.title: Process Termination
slides.notes: Next We will be learning about the Process Termination

slides.title: Process Termination
slides.notes: a process can terminate either voluntarily by calling exit() or involuntarily due to an error or a kill signal. When exit() is called, the operating system releases most of the process resources and returns an exit status to the parent. A status of 0 indicates success, while a non-zero value indicates an error. However, the process is completely removed only after the parent collects this status using wait().

slides.title: Process Termination
slides.notes: Like checking out of a hotel: you leave the room (release resources), but the front desk keeps your final bill on record until it’s settled.

slides.title: wait() - Synchronising Parent and Child
slides.notes: Next, the wait() system call is used for synchronization between parent and child processes. It makes the parent process pause execution until one of its child processes finishes. It also collects the exit status of the child, which allows the operating system to properly clean up the child’s process entry, known as the PCB, in a process called reaping. A more controlled version, waitpid(), allows the parent to wait for a specific child process instead of any child.

slides.title: wait() - Synchronising Parent and Child
slides.notes: A parent waiting up for their child to get home before locking the door — and, once home, asking how the day went (reading the exit status).

slides.title: Two Special Cases
slides.notes: Now, let's look at two special process states that occur because of the timing between a parent and child process. A Zombie process is one that has already finished execution, but its parent hasn't yet collected its exit status using wait(), so its process entry remains temporarily. An Orphan process, on the other hand, is created when the parent terminates before the child. In that case, the operating system reassigns the child to the init process (PID 1), which later waits for the child to finish and cleans up its process entry.
tables: Child has terminated, but the parent has NOT called wait() yet - its exit status is still on record
Keeps the child's process entry in the process table until the parent calls wait(), then removes it
The parent terminates BEFORE the child does
Reassigns the child to the init process (PID 1), which waits for it to terminate and then removes its process entry

slides.notes: Now, let's understand this with a timeline. The parent creates a child using fork(). If the child finishes execution before the parent calls wait(), it temporarily becomes a zombie process. Once the parent executes wait(), the operating system collects the child's exit status and removes the zombie entry.

slides.title: Orphan
slides.notes: Similarly, an orphan process is created when the parent terminates before the child. Instead of leaving the child unmanaged, the operating system reassigns it to the init process, which becomes its new parent. Once the child finishes execution, the init process calls wait() and cleans up the process entry.

slides.title: Zombies
slides.notes: Analogy: A zombie is a finished library book not yet checked back in — done, but still on the records.

slides.title: Putting It Together
slides.notes: Now we will be putting it all together.

slides.title: What Happens While Typing ls In Terminal?
slides.body:
The Full Cycle in Action
$ ls
Bash
slides.notes: Now, let’s put everything together with a real example: when you type ls in a terminal. 1 The shell, like Bash, first calls fork() to create a child process, which is initially a copy of the shell. 2 Then the child process uses exec() to replace itself with the ls program. 3 Meanwhile, the parent shell calls wait() so it pauses until ls finishes executing. 4 Once ls completes, it calls exit() and returns its status. 5 After that, the shell’s wait() call returns, and the prompt is shown again, ready for the next command.

slides.title: What Happens While Typing ls In Terminal?
slides.notes: Finally, let's put everything together with a real example. When you type ls in the terminal, the shell first creates a new process using fork(). The child then loads the ls program using exec() and executes it. After finishing, it calls exit(), while the parent waits using wait(). Once the child completes, the parent resumes execution and is ready to accept the next command.

Same PID; does not return on success
Parent waits for a child to finish and collects its status
Returns an exit status; frees resources

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.notes: Next we will understand the Context Switching

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.notes: Since a CPU core can execute only one process at a time, the operating system rapidly switches between processes to share CPU time. This switching is called a context switch. The “context” refers to the current state of a process, including things like the program counter, CPU registers, stack pointer, and memory information. This state is stored in the Process Control Block (PCB), so during a switch, the OS saves the current process state into its PCB and loads another process’s state from its PCB.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.body:
Save context
Restore context
Switching the CPU Between Processes
slides.notes: Analogy: A chef cooking several dishes on one stove: to switch from dish A to B, they jot down exactly where they stopped on A (save context), read their earlier notes for B (restore context), and carry on.

slides.title: The Mechanism - Save, Select, Restore
slides.notes: Next, let’s break down how a context switch actually happens. First, a trigger occurs—this could be a timer interrupt, a process waiting for I/O, a system call, or a higher-priority process becoming ready. Then the operating system saves the current process state into its PCB. After that, the scheduler selects the next process to run. Once selected, the OS restores that process’s saved state from its PCB. Finally, the CPU resumes execution of the new process exactly from where it had previously stopped.

slides.title: Context Switching
slides.notes: Now, let's follow the context switch step by step. Initially, P1 is executing while P2 is idle. When an interrupt or system call occurs, the CPU saves P1's state into its PCB and loads P2's saved state, allowing P2 to start executing. Later, another interrupt triggers the reverse process—the CPU saves P2's state, restores P1's state, and P1 resumes execution from exactly where it was interrupted.

slides.title: Switching Is Not Free
slides.notes: Finally, remember that context switching isn't free. While the operating system is saving and restoring process information, no user process is actually running, so that time becomes overhead. This overhead includes saving registers, updating the PCBs, and reloading the CPU cache and TLB for the next process.

slides.title: Switching Is Not Free
slides.notes: Moving on, if context switches happen too frequently, the CPU spends more time switching than actually executing processes, which is why choosing the right time slice is important. Also, switching between threads of the same process is cheaper than switching between different processes because the threads already share the same address space, so a full memory-map reload isn't required.
